Windowed sequence hyperedges: multi-way co-occurrence in coded sequences

honets

2026-08-25

The analytic question

Coded interaction sequences record one action at a time: a person specifies a requirement, the partner interrupts, a command follows. A transition network answers what follows what; a co-occurrence network answers which pairs appear together. Neither answers the question this tutorial takes up: which actions occur together as groups within short spans of activity, and do those groups recur often enough to constitute a structure?

A pairwise network cannot hold the answer, because a group of three actions inside one span is not the same observation as its three pairs. The hypergraph keeps the group intact: each short span of a sequence becomes one hyperedge over the distinct actions inside it. The construction follows Ding, Wang, Li, Li & Liu (2020); the resulting weighted incidence matrix carries edge-dependent vertex weights in the sense of Chitra & Raphael (2019), which the spectral machinery of Zhou, Huang & Schölkopf (2006) and Hayashi, Aksoy, Park & Park (2020) consumes directly.

The data are human_long, bundled with honets: 10,796 coded human turns from 429 human–AI pair-programming sessions, nine action codes, each code carrying an a-priori cluster label (Directive, Evaluative, Metacognitive) that the analysis below never uses — it will serve as an external check at the end.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

How a sequence becomes a hypergraph

Before the real data, a four-event sequence small enough to verify by hand. With window = 2 the windows are (a,b), (b,a), (a,c); the first two contain the same set of states, so they collapse into one hyperedge observed twice.

hg_tiny <- window_hypergraph(list(s1 = c("a", "b", "a", "c")), window = 2L)
as.data.frame(hg_tiny)
##   hyperedge size states weight
## 1        h1    2   a, b      2
## 2        h2    2   a, c      1

The table has one row per hyperedge. The set {a, b} was seen in 2 windows (weight = 2), the set {a, c} in 1. Weight is therefore recurrence: how many spans of the sequence produced exactly this combination. Repeats inside a window count as occurrences in the incidence matrix but not as extra members — a window (a, a) yields the singleton hyperedge {a} with an incidence cell of 2. This is what makes the incidence matrix edge-dependent-weighted rather than binary.

Recurrent action combinations in real sessions

Which combinations of actions recur inside three-turn spans of the sessions? The long format goes in directly: action names the code column, actor groups turns into sessions, time orders them.

hg_all <- window_hypergraph(human_long, action = "code",
                            actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",
                            window = 3L)
hg_all
## Hypergraph: 9 nodes, 129 hyperedges
## Size distribution:
##   size_1   : 9
##   size_2   : 36
##   size_3   : 84
## Source: windowed sequences, window = 3, step = 1 (9942 windows from 429 sequences)

The 429 sessions produce 9,942 windows (six sessions were shorter than three turns and contributed none — the constructor counts them rather than dropping them silently). The 129 hyperedges are exactly the 9 singletons, 36 pairs, and 84 triples that nine codes allow: with this much data, every possible combination occurs at least once. Presence alone is saturated, so any presence-based summary would be flat. The information is in the weights:

as.data.frame(hg_all, sort_by = "weight", top = 10)
##    hyperedge size                      states weight
## 1        h35    2            Command, Specify    722
## 2        h33    3   Command, Request, Specify    583
## 3       h124    2            Request, Specify    344
## 4        h26    3 Command, Interrupt, Specify    340
## 5       h120    2             Refine, Specify    295
## 6       h111    3 Interrupt, Request, Specify    265
## 7        h86    2          Frustrate, Specify    202
## 8       h118    3    Refine, Request, Specify    199
## 9        h21    3   Command, Inquire, Specify    190
## 10        h1    1                     Command    177

The distribution is far from flat. Command, Specify dominates with 722 windows, followed by Command, Request, Specify (583). Specify appears in eight of the top nine combinations: specification is the connective tissue of these sessions. The gap between the strongest combination (722) and the weakest (1) is what the saturated presence structure hides.

Since rare combinations are noise for structural analysis, the min_weight argument keeps only recurrent ones — the same role min_freq plays in higher-order rule extraction. Fifty windows out of 9,942 is a conservative floor; min_size = 2 also removes the nine singletons, which carry no co-occurrence information.

hg <- window_hypergraph(human_long, action = "code",
                        actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",
                        window = 3L, min_size = 2L, min_weight = 50L)
hg
## Hypergraph: 9 nodes, 56 hyperedges
## Size distribution:
##   size_2   : 22
##   size_3   : 34
## Source: windowed sequences, window = 3, step = 1 (9942 windows from 429 sequences)

Fifty-six combinations — 22 pairs and 34 triples — recur at least 50 times. This is the structure the rest of the analysis works on.

Seeing the recurrent combinations

splot(clique_expansion(hg_all), minimum = 0.05,
      title = "Windowed co-occurrence, projected")

How concentrated is the recurrent structure?

hypergraph_measures(hg)
## Hypergraph measures: 9 nodes, 56 hyperedges
##   Density:                0.2897
##   Mean edge size:         2.61
##   Pairwise participation: 0.9167
## 
##   Hyperdegree:    min=8  med=15.0  max=33
##   Node strength:  min=21.0  med=40.0  max=91.0
##   Edge sizes:     min=2  med=3.0  max=3
## 
## Intersection profile (pair counts by overlap size):
##   overlap_0   : 474
##   overlap_1   : 802
##   overlap_2   : 264

Three numbers matter here. First, hyperdegree now ranges from 8 to 33 (median 15): after filtering, the codes participate in very different numbers of recurrent combinations, where the unfiltered hypergraph had forced every code to the same value. Second, pairwise participation is 0.92 — almost every pair of codes still shares at least one recurrent hyperedge, so the structure is concentrated but not fragmented. Third, the intersection profile shows 264 hyperedge pairs overlapping in two codes: the triples are largely extensions of the strong pairs (for example Command, Specify extending to Command, Request, Specify), not separate formations.

Which actions anchor the combinations?

The H-eigenvector centrality of Benson (2019) scores each node on the uniform-size hypergraph tensor; unlike degree it rewards being in combinations whose other members are themselves central.

hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "H")
##        node         H
## 1   Command 0.3773413
## 2   Correct 0.3337657
## 3 Frustrate 0.3637328
## 4   Inquire 0.3340307
## 5 Interrupt 0.2831700
## 6    Refine 0.2820356
## 7   Request 0.3043738
## 8   Specify 0.4281911
## 9    Verify 0.2580999

Specify (0.43) is the clear anchor, with Command (0.38) second — the two directive actions sit inside most strong combinations. Verify (0.26), Refine (0.28), and Interrupt (0.28) are peripheral: they occur, and recur, but in combinations anchored by others. The ordering matches what the top-weight table already suggested, now as a single per-node score.

Do the actions organize into higher-order groups?

The random-walk Laplacian of Hayashi et al. (2020) uses both weight layers this hypergraph carries: the occurrence-count incidence (edge-dependent vertex weights) and the window counts, which hypergraph_cluster() picks up automatically as hyperedge weights. Spectral k-means is stochastic, so the run is seeded and repeated under a second seed as a stability check.

cl <- hypergraph_cluster(hg, k = 2L, type = "random_walk", seed = 1)
cl_check <- hypergraph_cluster(hg, k = 2L, type = "random_walk", seed = 99)
identical(as.data.frame(cl), as.data.frame(cl_check))
## [1] TRUE
as.data.frame(cl)
##        node   cluster         pi       dim1        dim2
## 1   Command Cluster 1 0.18476075 -0.7666588  0.64205472
## 2   Correct Cluster 2 0.07342118 -0.6251948 -0.78046872
## 3 Frustrate Cluster 2 0.08513619 -0.4829078 -0.87567123
## 4   Inquire Cluster 1 0.07212750 -0.8292714  0.55884608
## 5 Interrupt Cluster 1 0.07125103 -0.6293613  0.77711286
## 6    Refine Cluster 2 0.06733948 -0.4364170 -0.89974453
## 7   Request Cluster 1 0.10781145 -0.9215039  0.38836921
## 8   Specify Cluster 1 0.30937849 -0.9979768  0.06357931
## 9    Verify Cluster 1 0.02877393 -0.7116741  0.70250975

The partition is identical under both seeds, so it can be reported as stable. Cluster 2 is {Correct, Frustrate, Refine}; Cluster 1 is everything else, with Specify holding the largest stationary probability (pi = 0.31) — a random walker on the recurrent combinations spends almost a third of its time on Specify.

This is where the withheld labels come in: the coding scheme’s Evaluative cluster is {Correct, Frustrate, Refine, Verify}. The hypergraph recovered three of its four members from co-occurrence structure alone. The defector is informative: Verify co-occurs with Specify and Command (the combinations Command, Specify, Verify and Request, Specify, Verify each recur over 80 times), so within short spans verification behaves as part of the directive workflow, not the evaluative one.

plot(cl)

The embedding shows the same picture geometrically: the corrective codes separate on the second spectral dimension while Specify sits at the center of the main group.

Does the window size change the conclusions?

Window size is the one consequential arbitrary choice in this pipeline, so the headline result must survive a different value.

hg4 <- window_hypergraph(human_long, action = "code",
                         actor = "session_id", time = "timestamp",
                         window = 4L, min_size = 2L, min_weight = 50L)
as.data.frame(hg4, sort_by = "weight", top = 8)
##   hyperedge size                               states weight
## 1       h24    3            Command, Request, Specify    447
## 2       h20    3          Command, Interrupt, Specify    357
## 3       h26    2                     Command, Specify    343
## 4       h19    4 Command, Interrupt, Request, Specify    241
## 5       h50    3             Refine, Request, Specify    221
## 6       h17    3            Command, Inquire, Specify    212
## 7        h8    3            Command, Correct, Specify    173
## 8       h52    2                     Request, Specify    168

With four-turn windows the same combinations lead: Command, Request, Specify (447), Command, Interrupt, Specify (357), Command, Specify (343), and their four-code extension Command, Interrupt, Request, Specify now enters at 241 — wider windows admit larger sets, but the membership of the dominant combinations is unchanged. The conclusion — directive combinations anchored by Specify dominate, corrective actions form their own block — does not depend on the choice of three versus four.

When to use which

  • window_hypergraph() — sequences, and the question is about combinations local in time. step = 1 (sliding) weights every span; step = window (tumbling) counts disjoint spans and suits length comparisons across groups. Raise min_weight before structural analysis on dense data; this tutorial’s saturation of all 129 possible sets is the norm, not the exception, once windows are plentiful.
  • group_hypergraph() — the grouping is already categorical (a whole session, a document, a team) and position in time is irrelevant. A whole-sequence window reproduces it exactly.
  • build_hypergraph() — the input is an estimated pairwise network and the hyperedges should be its cliques.
  • clique_expansion() — hands the hypergraph back to pairwise machinery (Nestimate, cograph) when a graph method is needed; the multi-way distinctions collapse into edge weights at that point, which is exactly what this tutorial’s construction exists to avoid.

References

  • Benson, A. R. (2019). Three hypergraph eigenvector centralities. SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science, 1(2), 293–312.
  • Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights. ICML 2019, PMLR 97, 1172–1181.
  • Ding, K., Wang, J., Li, J., Li, D., & Liu, H. (2020). Be more with less: Hypergraph attention networks for inductive text classification. EMNLP 2020, 4927–4936.
  • Hayashi, K., Aksoy, S. G., Park, C. H., & Park, H. (2020). Hypergraph random walks, Laplacians, and clustering. CIKM 2020, 495–504.
  • Zhou, D., Huang, J., & Schölkopf, B. (2006). Learning with hypergraphs: Clustering, classification, and embedding. NeurIPS 2006, 1601–1608.
